gre-verbal.title: GRE Verbal — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
gre-verbal.summary: Master Reading Comprehension, Text Completion, and Sentence Equivalence to score 160+.

slides.title: What is GRE Verbal?
points: Tests reading comprehension, vocabulary in context, and logical reasoning
Two sections, 20 questions each, 30 minutes per section
Adaptive: second section difficulty depends on first-section performance
Score range: 130–170 (scale changed post-2023)

example.label: Format Overview
example.text: Verbal Reasoning = 40 questions across 2 sections; one essay-reading comprehension pair may have multiple questions

slides.tip: Adaptive scoring rewards accuracy on harder questions; don't rush to finish.

slides.title: Verbal Section Timing & Strategy
points: 30 minutes for 20 questions ≈ 1.5 min/question average
Text Completion: 30 seconds. Sentence Equivalence: 45 seconds. Reading: 2–3 min per passage
Read the question/prompt FIRST before reading full text
Flag unknowns; come back after easier questions if time permits
slides.tip: Pacing is critical. Practice timed sections to build speed without sacrificing accuracy.
slides.warn: Avoid guessing randomly; eliminate wrong answers systematically.

slides.title: Text Completion Overview
points: Fill in 1–3 blanks in a sentence or short passage
Logic clues (contrast, causation, parallelism) hint at the answer
Single-blank: straightforward meaning. Multi-blank: all blanks must fit
~20% of Verbal section

example.label: Single-Blank Example
example.text: Despite her _____ demeanor, she was known for her sharp intellect. (A) affable (B) acerbic (C) candid) → Answer: (A) affable, contrasts with 'despite' + 'sharp intellect'

slides.tip: Cover the choices first; predict your own answer, then match.

slides.title: Text Completion: Multi-Blank Mastery
points: Identify relationships between blanks (same direction or opposite)
Eliminate one blank pair at a time if stuck
Punctuation and conjunctions signal logic flow
One wrong blank invalidates the whole answer

example.label: Two-Blank Example
example.text: The CEO's _____ approach to innovation was both _____ and risky. (A) cautious...prudent (B) audacious...reckless (C) deliberate...conservative → Answer: (B) or (C) fit, but (B) better captures 'risky'

slides.tip: Start with the blank that feels most constrained by context.

slides.title: Sentence Equivalence Strategy
points: Pick TWO words that create the SAME meaning in the sentence
Not synonyms alone; they must produce identical sentence logic
~10% of Verbal. Same difficulty as Text Completion blanks
6 choices, only one correct pair

example.label: Sentence Equivalence Example
example.text: The critic's _____ remarks about the film were surprising given her previous praise. (A) acerbic (B) caustic (C) favorable (D) laudatory (E) scathing (F) encomium → Answer: (A) acerbic + (E) scathing (both mean harsh/cutting)

slides.tip: Eliminate pairs that don't both fit; focus on primary definition fit first.

slides.title: Reading Comprehension Basics
points: ~50% of Verbal section; passages: 1 short (100 words), 1–2 medium (250–400 words)
Question types: main idea, inference, author's tone, sentence function, vocabulary
Adaptive CAT: harder passages = more points per correct answer
Active reading: underline topic sentences, contrasts, claims

example.label: Passage Structure
example.text: Intro (thesis) → Evidence 1 → Counter/nuance → Evidence 2 → Conclusion. Typical academic journal format

slides.tip: Read the passage first (don't skim), then tackle questions without re-reading full text unless asked.

slides.title: Reading: Main Idea & Author's Purpose
points: Main idea: the overarching claim, not just the topic
Author's purpose: to argue, explain, criticize, defend, compare
Avoid overly broad or narrow summaries
Watch for 'which of the following best' — not just 'true,' but BEST

example.label: Wrong vs. Right
example.text: Wrong: 'The passage is about photosynthesis.' Right: 'The author argues that recent discoveries have fundamentally changed our understanding of photosynthesis efficiency.'

slides.tip: State the main idea in one sentence before checking answer choices.

slides.title: Reading: Inference & Detail Questions
points: Inference: what logically follows from the text (not stated directly)
Detail: what is explicitly mentioned (safe to reference by line number)
Distinguish between 'author implies' and 'author states'
Use line references to eliminate ambiguity

example.label: Inference Example
example.text: Text: 'The study found no correlation between variable X and outcome Y.' Inference: 'The researchers likely had a hypothesis linking X and Y, but data contradicted it.'

slides.tip: For inference, never go beyond one logical step; avoid wild extrapolations.

slides.title: Reading: Tone, Attitude & Author's Stance
points: Tone: How does the author SOUND? Critical, supportive, neutral, skeptical?
Tone ≠ topic. A neutral treatment of controversial material is possible
Watch for qualifiers: 'arguably,' 'perhaps,' 'some scholars believe' → hedging
Single-word tone labels: didactic, pedantic, sardonic, nostalgic, etc.

example.label: Tone Recognition
example.text: 'The proponents of this theory claim...' (skeptical/distant) vs. 'The elegant theory explains...' (supportive/appreciative)

slides.tip: Identify adjectives/adverbs the author uses to describe ideas; they reveal stance.

slides.title: Reading: Function & Rhetorical Questions
points: Why did the author include this sentence/phrase? (Not what does it mean)
Function: introduces example, concedes a point, strengthens argument, etc.
Rhetorical questions: posed for effect, not to be answered directly
Transitions (however, moreover, instead) signal shifts in function

example.label: Function Example
example.text: Sentence: 'Even critics concede that the method is cost-effective.' Function: Acknowledge counterargument to strengthen main claim

slides.tip: Restate the function in gerund form: 'introducing,' 'contrasting,' 'supporting.'

slides.title: Vocabulary Strategy for Verbal
points: GRE rewards high-frequency, nuanced words (not obscure memorization)
Root-based learning: Latin/Greek roots unlock meaning of related words
Context clues: synonyms, antonyms, definitions, examples in text
Use Anki or flashcard decks for 500+ GRE-common words

example.label: Root Mastery
example.text: Root 'mal-' (bad): malady, malign, malapropism, malevolent. Learn one root = 10+ words

slides.tip: For unknown words, look for structural clues (prefix/suffix) before guessing.

slides.title: Verbal: Common Trap Answers
points: Synonym bait: sounds right but doesn't fit the blank context
Extreme language: 'always,' 'never,' 'all,' 'none' often incorrect
Author's opinion confusion: picking what author believes, not what passage claims
Literal vs. figurative: passage may use metaphor; answer is literal

example.label: Trap Example
example.text: Blank: 'His speech was _____.' Choices: (A) brief (B) terse. Both mean short, but 'terse' = curtly short, 'brief' = simply short. Context determines fit

slides.warn: Never pick an answer because it's a real word; it must fit the specific sentence logic.

slides.title: Passage Mapping for Efficiency
points: For longer passages, write a one-line summary per paragraph
Mark paragraph numbers and main idea on test booklet
Highlight contrast/counter-arguments (signal words: 'but,' 'yet,' 'however')
Reduces re-reading time on inference and tone questions

example.label: Passage Map Sample
example.text: Para 1: Historical background. Para 2: Traditional view (wrong). Para 3: New evidence. Para 4: Implications.

slides.tip: Spend 2 min reading + mapping; save 1 min on 3–4 questions.

slides.title: Short vs. Long Reading Passages
points: Short (~100 words): 1 question, high precision needed; re-read if uncertain
Long (~350 words): 3–4 questions, multiple-choice or select-all-that-apply
Select-all: pick every true statement (not 'best' — all correct count)
If unsure on select-all, safer to pick fewer and recheck logic

example.label: Select-All Example
example.text: Q: 'Which of the following are true?' (A) Author criticizes theory. (B) Study supports theory. (C) Both A & B are stated. → Pick all that apply based on text

slides.tip: For select-all, verify each choice independently before submitting.

slides.title: Comparison & Parallel Passage Reading
points: Two passages (200–300 words each) on related topics
Questions ask: similarity, difference, author's relationship, implicit connection
Passage A vs. Passage B comparison: read both fully before answering
Avoid conflating the two; each author has distinct voice/intent

example.label: Comparison Q
example.text: Passage A: 'Theory X is outdated.' Passage B: 'Theory X remains relevant.' Q: How do authors differ? → Contradictory positions

slides.tip: Mark agreement/disagreement zones for quick comparison-question reference.

slides.title: Analytical vs. Opinion Questions
points: Analytical: factual; grounded in passage statements or clear inferences
Opinion: speculation about author's beliefs; dangerous unless clearly signaled
GRE favors analytical; opinions only if passage explicitly states belief
Phrases: 'author likely believes' vs. 'author explicitly states' — big difference

example.label: Analytical vs. Opinion
example.text: Text: 'The data shows a correlation.' Analytical: 'A correlation exists.' Opinion: 'The author thinks causation is likely.'

slides.warn: Avoid inferring author's intent beyond what the passage supports.

slides.title: Sentence Completion in Context
points: Rarely standalone; usually within a passage (2–3 sentences surrounding blank)
Use full context: the sentence before and after guide meaning
Parallel structure often signals the answer (same part of speech, tense)
Not about vocabulary; it's about logical fit

example.label: Context Example
example.text: Prior: 'She had worked tirelessly.' Blank: 'Her _____ efforts.' Parallel: 'tireless,' 'relentless' fit; 'lazy' doesn't, despite being a real adjective

slides.tip: Use surrounding sentences to narrow options before guessing.

slides.title: Critical Reading: Bias & Subjectivity
points: All authors have a perspective; identify their lens (scientific, political, personal)
Bias ≠ bad; a biased argument can be well-reasoned
Watch for loaded language: 'obviously,' 'clearly,' 'undoubtedly' → author asserting without proof
GRE tests your ability to recognize and evaluate bias, not to condemn it

example.label: Bias Recognition
example.text: Author A: 'The evidence clearly shows...' vs. Author B: 'Some scholars argue...' → A is more assertive/opinionated

slides.tip: Distinguish between author's claim and its validity; GRE rewards objectivity in analysis.

slides.title: Verbal Scoring & Your Target
points: Scale: 130 (no correct) to 170 (all correct); ~1 point per question correct on average
160+: ~35–36 correct per section. 150+: ~28–29 correct per section
Adaptive: easier 2nd section if you miss many in 1st; harder 2nd if you do well
Each correct answer on harder questions = more points (hidden scoring)

example.label: Score Breakdown
example.text: 30/40 correct = ~160–163. 35/40 correct = ~168–170. Difficulty of correct answers varies the exact score

slides.tip: Aim for 75%+ accuracy (30/40) to hit 160+; perfectionism isn't required.

slides.title: Top 5 Verbal Mistakes
points: Rushing through reading; missing nuance costs 3–5 points per passage
Vocabulary guessing without context; GRE tests words in context, not isolation
Over-inferring; going 2–3 logical steps beyond text
Ignoring negation ('not,' 'neither,' 'except') in questions; flips meaning
Freezing on a hard question; skip and return with fresh eyes
slides.tip: Practice under timed conditions to internalize pacing and avoid panic skipping.
slides.warn: Wrong answers are often partially correct; they test your discernment, not guessing.

slides.title: Practice Strategy for Verbal
points: Week 1–2: untimed; focus on understanding question types and logic
Week 3–4: section practice at 30 min per section; build speed
Week 5–6: full tests under exam conditions (adaptive CAT simulations)
Review errors: categorize by type (vocab, inference, pacing) and drill weak areas

example.label: Weekly Drill
example.text: Monday: 10 Text Completions (untimed). Tuesday: 5 Reading passages (timed). Wed–Fri: mixed section drills. Weekend: full 40-question section

slides.tip: Use official ETS PowerPrep tests; unofficial materials may not reflect real difficulty.

slides.title: Free GRE Verbal Mocks & Resources
points: ETS PowerPrep+ (free two full tests): https://www.ets.org/gre/revised_general/prepare
Magoosh GRE Vocabulary app: 1000+ words with spaced repetition
Manhattan Prep 5-lb. book: 1000+ practice questions by type
Read quality articles: The Economist, Scientific American, academic journals

example.label: Reading Practice
example.text: Read one Economist article daily; time yourself; answer comprehension Qs without re-reading. Builds speed & retention

slides.tip: Complement formal prep with 10–15 min daily reading of challenging material.

slides.title: GRE Verbal: Final Tips
points: Confidence matters: familiar question types save mental energy
Adaptive CAT exploits hesitation; make decisions decisively, move forward
On test day: read carefully, eliminate aggressively, skip strategically
Post-test: review wrong answers for patterns, not just correct answers
slides.tip: A high Verbal score (160+) takes practice; consistency beats last-minute cramming.
slides.warn: Vocabulary growth takes months; start prep 3–4 months before test if English is non-native.

slides.title: Next: Free GRE Mock Tests
points: Take a full adaptive mock this week to measure baseline
Review Verbal section errors in detail
Target 3–4 more mocks over 6–8 weeks
Use results to refine your strategy and timing

example.label: Mock Test Schedule
example.text: Week 1: Baseline mock. Weeks 2–3: Focused drills. Week 4: Mock 2. Weeks 5–6: Intensive review. Week 7: Mock 3. Week 8: Final test

slides.tip: Our Codex platform offers AI-powered GRE Verbal drills and personalized feedback. Start free today!

gre-quant.title: GRE Quant — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
gre-quant.summary: Conquer Quantitative Comparison, Numeric Entry, and Data Interpretation to score 165+.

slides.title: What is GRE Quant?
points: Tests math reasoning, problem-solving, and data interpretation
Two sections, 20 questions each, 35 minutes per section
Adaptive: second section difficulty depends on first-section performance
Score range: 130–170 (post-2023 shortened GRE)

example.label: Question Types Breakdown
example.text: Quantitative Comparison (QC): ~7 q/section. Multiple-choice/multiple-answers: ~10 q/section. Numeric Entry: ~2 q/section. Data Interpretation: ~1 q/section

slides.tip: No calculator on many older GRE tests, but modern version allows calculator on-screen for all Quant.

slides.title: Quant Section Timing & Strategy
points: 35 minutes for 20 questions ≈ 1.75 min/question average
Quantitative Comparison: 60–90 seconds. Multiple-choice: 90–120 seconds. Numeric: 60 seconds
Harder questions at end; allocate more time if adaptive sends you there
Skip and return strategy: if stuck >90 sec, flag and move on
slides.tip: Use on-screen calculator for arithmetic; save mental energy for strategy.
slides.warn: Calculator speeds some problems but can create false confidence; always estimate first.

slides.title: Quantitative Comparison (QC) Basics
points: Compare Quantity A vs. Quantity B; choose A > B, A < B, A = B, or 'cannot be determined'
~35% of Quant section; tests reasoning more than computation
No calculator advantage; focus on structure and comparison logic
Answer (D) 'cannot be determined' is rare (~10% of QC); be suspicious

example.label: Simple QC Example
example.text: Quantity A: sqrt(144). Quantity B: 12. Answer: (C) The quantities are equal

slides.tip: Plug in numbers (especially negatives, zero, fractions) to find cases where A vs. B changes.

slides.title: QC Strategy: Canceling Common Terms
points: If both A and B contain the same factor or term, cancel it
Reduces complexity; compare what remains
Example: A = 2x+5, B = 3x+5. Cancel 5; compare 2x vs. 3x (depends on sign of x)
Useful for algebraic QC; saves computation time

example.label: Canceling Example
example.text: A: 1/7 + 1/8. B: 2/15. Find common denominator? No. Compare numerically: A ≈ 0.018 + 0.125 = 0.143 > B ≈ 0.133. Answer: A > B

slides.tip: Cancel only when you're certain both quantities contain the term; don't cancel blindly.

slides.title: QC Trap: Testing Edge Cases
points: Negative vs. positive: if x appears, test x > 0 and x < 0 separately
Zero: if x ≥ 0 allowed, test x = 0
Fractions: test x = 1/2, x = 2; different outcomes from integers
If outcome changes based on the value, answer is (D) 'cannot be determined'

example.label: Edge Case Flip
example.text: A: x². B: x. If x = 0: A = B = 0. If x = 2: A = 4 > B = 2. If x = -1: A = 1 > B = -1. Answer: (D) cannot be determined (depends on x)

slides.warn: Many QC problems hinge on one edge case; always test at least {-1, 0, 1, 1/2, 2}.

slides.title: Multiple-Choice (Single Answer)
points: Pick one best answer from 5 choices
~40% of Quant; tests calculation, interpretation, and reasoning
Read carefully: 'which of the following,' 'the most nearly equal,' 'approximately'
Use estimation to eliminate extremes quickly

example.label: Estimation Example
example.text: Q: If 7x + 3 = 52, what is x? A) 6 B) 7 C) 8 D) 9 E) 10. Solve: 7x = 49, x = 7. Answer: (B)

slides.tip: Even if you can solve, estimate answer range first to catch calculation errors.

slides.title: Multiple-Choice: Multiple Answers (Select All)
points: Select all answers that satisfy the condition
No partial credit; all correct boxes checked = points, any error = 0
Typically 2–3 correct answers out of 5–7 choices
Verify each choice independently; don't assume pattern from first correct one

example.label: Select-All Example
example.text: Q: Which of the following are divisible by 3? (A) 9 (B) 15 (C) 22 (D) 27 (E) 30. Answer: (A), (B), (D), (E). Test: 9/3=3✓, 15/3=5✓, 22/3=7.33✗, 27/3=9✓, 30/3=10✓

slides.tip: Recheck your logic before clicking 'confirm'; all-or-nothing means zero tolerance for slips.

slides.title: Numeric Entry (Fill-in-the-Blank)
points: Type exact numerical answer; no multiple choices
~10% of Quant; often tests final calculation (last step of multi-step problem)
Units may or may not be requested; read carefully
Decimals and fractions both accepted; round only if instructed

example.label: Numeric Entry Example
example.text: Q: If a rectangle has length 5 and width 3, what is its area? Answer: Type 15 (no unit unless asked)

slides.tip: Double-check your arithmetic; there's no answer-choice check, only your calculation.

slides.title: Numeric Entry: Rounding & Precision
points: If the question says 'round to the nearest integer,' enter 7 not 7.0
If it says 'round to the nearest hundredth,' enter 3.14 (not 3.1 or 3.1400)
Some answers are exact (fractions): 1/2 is better than 0.5 if fractions accepted
Check the instructions; they change what you enter

example.label: Rounding Precision
example.text: 2/3 ≈ 0.667. If asked for nearest hundredth: 0.67. If exact answer requested: 2/3

slides.warn: Rounding errors (entering 0.6667 instead of 0.67) will be marked wrong.

slides.title: Data Interpretation Basics
points: Read charts, tables, graphs, and extract quantitative information
~5% of Quant (1 question per section, often a multi-part set)
Typical formats: bar chart, line graph, scatterplot, table, two-way frequency table
Questions ask: trends, comparisons, calculations from the data

example.label: Data Interpretation Sample
example.text: Table: Sales by quarter. Q: Which quarter had the highest sales? A: Read max value from table. Q: What was the % increase from Q1 to Q2? A: (Q2-Q1)/Q1 × 100

slides.tip: Read axis labels and legends carefully; mislabeling is a common trap.

slides.title: Arithmetic Fundamentals
points: Order of operations: PEMDAS (Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply/Divide, Add/Subtract)
Fractions: addition (common denominator), multiplication (numerator × numerator, denominator × denominator)
Decimals: align decimal points when adding/subtracting; count places when multiplying
Percentages: part = (percent/100) × whole
slides.tip: Master fraction ↔ decimal ↔ percent conversions; GRE loves mixing formats.

slides.title: Algebra: Equations & Variables
points: Solve for x: isolate variable on one side using inverse operations
Quadratic equations: factor, complete the square, or use quadratic formula
Inequalities: reverse inequality sign when multiplying/dividing by negative
Systems: substitute or eliminate; pick the faster method

example.label: Quadratic Example
example.text: x² - 5x + 6 = 0. Factor: (x-2)(x-3) = 0. Solutions: x = 2 or x = 3. Verify: 4 - 10 + 6 = 0 ✓

slides.tip: Always check solutions by substituting back into the original equation.

slides.title: Geometry Essentials: Shapes & Area
points: Rectangle: Area = length × width. Perimeter = 2(l + w)
Triangle: Area = (1/2) × base × height. Angles sum to 180°
Circle: Area = πr². Circumference = 2πr. Sector angle/360 = area/total area
Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c² for right triangles

example.label: Right Triangle
example.text: Sides 3, 4, and ?: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5². Hypotenuse = 5. Area = (1/2) × 3 × 4 = 6

slides.tip: Memorize common Pythagorean triples: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25).

slides.title: Geometry: Volume & 3D
points: Rectangular box: Volume = length × width × height. Surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh)
Cylinder: Volume = πr²h. Surface area = 2πr² + 2πrh
Sphere: Volume = (4/3)πr³. Surface area = 4πr²
Cone: Volume = (1/3)πr²h

example.label: Cylinder Volume
example.text: Radius 2, height 5: V = π × 2² × 5 = 20π ≈ 62.8

slides.tip: GRE rarely asks obscure formulas; these are the main ones. Memorize and practice.

slides.title: Word Problems: Setting Up Equations
points: Read twice: once for overall sense, again for specific numbers/unknowns
Define variables clearly: let x = unknown quantity
Translate English to math: 'is' → =, 'product' → ×, 'sum' → +, 'more than' → +
Solve and verify: plug answer back into the problem

example.label: Distance-Rate-Time Example
example.text: Tom travels 60 mph for 2 hours, then 40 mph for 3 hours. Total distance? D = 60(2) + 40(3) = 120 + 120 = 240 miles

slides.tip: Draw a diagram (distance line, work table, Venn diagram) for complex word problems.

slides.title: Word Problems: Work & Rate
points: Work rate: (1/time) = (1/rate). Combined: 1/total = 1/A + 1/B
If A does a job in 4 hours, rate = 1/4 job per hour
Two workers: combined rate = 1/4 + 1/6 = 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12 job per hour
Time to finish together = 12/5 = 2.4 hours

example.label: Two-Worker Problem
example.text: Alice paints a room in 6 hours. Bob paints it in 4 hours. Together? Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/4 = 2/12 + 3/12 = 5/12. Time = 12/5 = 2.4 hours

slides.tip: Always use the reciprocal of time for rates; add rates, then take reciprocal of sum for combined time.

slides.title: Probability & Counting
points: Probability = (favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes). Range: 0 to 1
Counting: permutations (order matters) = n!/(n-r)!. Combinations (order doesn't) = n! / (r!(n-r)!)
AND rule: multiply probabilities (if independent). OR rule: add (mutually exclusive)
Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B)

example.label: Combination Example
example.text: Pick 2 colors from 5. Combinations = 5!/(2!3!) = (5×4)/(2×1) = 10 ways. Order doesn't matter (red-blue = blue-red)

slides.tip: Distinguish permutations (order matters) from combinations; most GRE questions use combinations.

slides.title: Statistics: Mean, Median, Mode, Range
points: Mean (average): sum / count. Affected by outliers
Median (middle): arrange in order, pick middle value. Not affected by outliers
Mode (most frequent): most common value. May have none or multiple
Range: max - min. Measures spread

example.label: Stats Example
example.text: Data: 1, 2, 2, 5, 100. Mean = 110/5 = 22. Median = 2. Mode = 2. Range = 100 - 1 = 99. (Mean is skewed by outlier 100)

slides.tip: Median is more robust to outliers; use it when extreme values exist in the data.

slides.title: Statistics: Standard Deviation & Variance
points: Variance: average squared distance from mean
Standard deviation: square root of variance; measures spread in same units as data
Low SD = data clustered near mean. High SD = data spread out
GRE rarely asks for calculation; more about interpretation and comparison

example.label: SD Interpretation
example.text: Test A: mean 80, SD 5. Test B: mean 80, SD 15. Both have same average, but B's scores are more spread out

slides.tip: Understand that ±1 SD includes ~68% of data; ±2 SD includes ~95% (normal distribution).

slides.title: Calculator Tips & Pitfalls
points: Use calculator for arithmetic, not strategy. Think first, calculate second
Common error: forgetting order of operations with calculator input
Estimation first: rough answer in head, then refine with calculator
Watch for decimal-point misplacement: 0.123 vs. 12.3 vs. 123

example.label: Calculator Pitfall
example.text: Compute (5 + 3) × 2. Wrong: 5 + 3 × 2 = 5 + 6 = 11. Right: (5+3) × 2 = 8 × 2 = 16. Use parentheses!

slides.warn: Calculator speeds computation but doesn't replace thinking; lazy calculation leads to careless errors.

slides.title: Quant Scoring & Target
points: Scale: 130 (0 correct) to 170 (all 40 correct); ~1 point per question
Adaptive: second section difficulty = feedback from first-section performance
Harder questions = more points each; perfection isn't required to score 160+

example.label: Score Estimate
example.text: 35/40 correct = ~167. 32/40 correct = ~162. 30/40 correct = ~160. (Exact score depends on difficulty of correct answers)

slides.tip: Aim for 80%+ accuracy (32/40) to hit 160+; prioritize accuracy over speed.

slides.title: Top 5 Quant Mistakes
points: Misreading the question: 'which is NOT' vs. 'which IS' changes answer completely
Careless arithmetic: order of operations, decimal misplacement, sign errors
Skipping the setup: jumping to calculation without understanding the problem
Ignoring units: answer is 240 feet, not 240; units matter
Over-trusting calculator: GRE tests reasoning; easy to auto-pilot through wrong approach
slides.tip: Re-read the question after solving; verify you answered what was asked.
slides.warn: Most Quant errors are careless, not conceptual. Slow down, double-check arithmetic.

slides.title: Practice Strategy for Quant
points: Week 1–2: drill by topic (arithmetic, algebra, geometry) untimed
Week 3–4: mixed-topic, timed sections (35 min per 20 q)
Week 5–6: full adaptive CAT mocks under test conditions
Review: categorize errors (concept, arithmetic, reading) and restudy weak topics

example.label: Weekly Quant Schedule
example.text: Mon: 10 QC (Quant Comparison). Tue: 8 word problems. Wed: 5 data interpretation. Thu–Fri: mixed drills. Sat: full section. Sun: review errors

slides.tip: Use official ETS PowerPrep+ for realistic difficulty; third-party prep may be harder or easier than real GRE.

slides.title: Free GRE Quant Mocks & Resources
points: ETS PowerPrep+ (free): https://www.ets.org/gre/revised_general/prepare
Khan Academy GRE Math: free video lessons on all topics (arithmetic to geometry)
GMAT Club forums: unofficial problems with detailed solutions
Magoosh GRE Math: 600+ practice problems with video explanations

example.label: Free Resource Combo
example.text: Monday: Khan Academy video on algebra. Tue–Thu: problem drills (GMAT Club or Magoosh free trial). Fri: timed section. Sat: full mock (PowerPrep)

slides.tip: Start with Khan Academy if you need conceptual review; then move to practice problems.

slides.title: GRE Quant: Final Tips
points: Confidence = speed. Familiar concepts reduce cognitive load
Adaptive CAT: every question is harder/easier based on your prior performance
If you encounter a very hard section, you're likely doing well; don't panic
On test day: pace yourself, estimate before calculating, verify answers
slides.tip: A high Quant score (160+) requires deep fluency in fundamentals; cramming formulas won't suffice.
slides.warn: Quant is skill-building; start prep 8–12 weeks before test if math is weak.

slides.title: Next: Free GRE Mock Tests
points: Take a full adaptive mock to measure Quant baseline
Review errors: concept gaps vs. careless mistakes
Drill weak topics 3–5 times per week for 4–6 weeks
Retake a full mock every 2 weeks to track improvement

example.label: Mock Test Iteration
example.text: Week 1: Baseline mock. Identify weak topic (e.g., geometry). Weeks 2–3: Daily geometry drills. Week 4: Mock 2 to retest. Repeat for next weak topic

gre-writing.title: GRE Analytical Writing — Tips, Tricks & Strategy
gre-writing.summary: Craft compelling essays to score 5.0+ on the Analyze an Issue task.

slides.title: What is GRE Analytical Writing (AWA)?
points: One timed essay: 'Analyze an Issue.' 30 minutes to read prompt, plan, and write
Score: 0–6 (half-point increments). No multiple-choice; human and AI graders evaluate
~5% of total application weight (Verbal & Quant are 50% each)
Required for all GRE test-takers; few schools emphasize AWA beyond 'submitted'

example.label: AWA Task
example.text: Prompt: 'Some argue that technology isolates people; others say it connects them. Discuss both views and take a position.' Write ~400–500 words in 30 minutes

slides.tip: AWA is often overlooked by students; a strong essay (5.5–6) can stand out, especially for admission borderline cases.

slides.title: Scoring Rubric: What Graders Look For
points: Thesis clarity: do you take a clear, defensible stance? (Not neutral fence-sitting)
Evidence & examples: specific, relevant examples (not vague generalizations)
Reasoning: logical flow; how do your ideas connect? (Avoid non-sequiturs)
Writing quality: grammar, vocabulary, clarity, sentence variety

example.label: Scoring Breakdown
example.text: 6 = insightful thesis + strong evidence + sophisticated reasoning. 5 = clear thesis + adequate evidence + good reasoning. 4 = adequate thesis + some evidence + okay reasoning. <4 = unclear thesis or weak evidence

slides.tip: Graders prioritize clear thesis and evidence; perfect grammar matters less than coherent argument.

slides.title: Essay Structure: The 5-Paragraph Formula
points: Paragraph 1 (Intro): acknowledge both viewpoints, state your thesis clearly (1–2 sentences)
Paragraphs 2–3 (Body): each presents one strand of your argument with specific example
Paragraph 4: counter-argument or limitation; show you've thought deeply
Paragraph 5 (Conclusion): restate thesis, summarize key points, broader implication

example.label: Structure Template
example.text: Intro: 'While both technology's isolating and connecting effects are valid, connection ultimately outweighs isolation because [thesis].' Body 1: Evidence of connection. Body 2: Response to isolation concern. Conclusion: Thesis + implications

slides.tip: 5 paragraphs is a safe baseline; 4–6 paragraphs are all acceptable if ideas flow logically.

slides.title: Crafting a Strong Thesis
points: Take a clear side: 'agree,' 'disagree,' or 'nuanced position' (e.g., 'mostly agree but...')
Avoid fence-sitting: 'both views have merit' is weak; specify WHY your side is stronger
One sentence, if possible: readers (and graders) want immediate clarity
Establish scope: 'in modern education' is stronger than 'always and everywhere'

example.label: Thesis Examples
example.text: Weak: 'Technology has both positive and negative effects.' Strong: 'While technology creates some isolation risks, its capacity to facilitate global collaboration and access to information makes it a net positive force in society.'

slides.tip: Your thesis is your argument's skeleton; everything else hangs on it. Make it explicit.

slides.title: Evidence: Specific Examples vs. Generalizations
points: Use concrete examples: 'Social media platforms like LinkedIn enable professionals to collaborate across continents'
Avoid vague claims: 'Technology is great' has zero credibility
Personal experience is valid: 'I used video conferencing to work with a team across three countries'
Hypothetical scenarios: 'Imagine a student without internet access vs. one with unlimited bandwidth...'

example.label: Example Strength
example.text: Weak: 'Technology helps people.' Strong: 'The rise of telemedicine has allowed rural patients to consult specialist doctors without traveling hundreds of miles, reducing both cost and time barriers.'

slides.tip: Every claim needs at least one supporting example; graders downgrade essays that assert without evidence.

slides.title: Building Your Argument: Logical Flow
points: Claim → Evidence → Analysis (so what?). Don't just list examples; explain their relevance
Topic sentences: start each body paragraph with a claim, then support it
Transitions: 'Furthermore,' 'In contrast,' 'However,' 'To illustrate' guide readers through logic
Avoid logical fallacies: hasty generalization, false cause, ad hominem, strawman

example.label: Logical Flow
example.text: Claim: 'Technology enables global collaboration.' Evidence: 'Open-source software projects like Linux involve thousands of developers across continents.' Analysis: 'This demonstrates that technology removes geographic barriers, allowing diverse talent to pool expertise in ways previously impossible.'

slides.tip: After writing, read your essay aloud; if the logic feels choppy, add transitions or reorganize paragraphs.

slides.title: Counter-Argument & Nuance
points: Acknowledge the opposing view: show intellectual honesty and depth
Concede valid points: 'It is true that social media can foster addiction.' Then reframe
Distinguish your position: 'However, the benefits of information access outweigh addiction risks if users practice digital literacy'
Avoid strawmanning: don't misrepresent the other side

example.label: Concession & Reframe
example.text: Opposing view: 'Technology isolates people by replacing face-to-face interaction.' Your counter: 'While some isolation risk exists, technology enables isolated individuals (rural, disabled, homebound) to build communities they could never access offline. The net effect is greater connection.'

slides.tip: A 6-level essay engages both sides thoughtfully; a 5-level essay may ignore counter-arguments.

slides.title: Writing Quality: Vocabulary & Clarity
points: Vary sentence length: mix short + long sentences to maintain reader engagement
Use precise verbs: 'facilitate' is stronger than 'help'; 'exacerbate' vs. 'make worse'
Avoid jargon: clarity beats sophistication; if you use technical terms, define them
Proofread: minor grammar errors don't tank a score, but many errors do

example.label: Vocabulary Upgrade
example.text: Weak: 'Technology is good because it helps people.' Better: 'Technology democratizes access to knowledge and facilitates collaboration, fundamentally reshaping how people learn and work.'

slides.tip: You don't need $5 vocabulary; clear, direct writing beats flowery language with errors.

slides.title: Common Writing Mistakes in AWA
points: Lack of clear thesis: grader struggles to identify your position
Unsupported claims: assertions without examples collapse under scrutiny
Repetition: restating the same point in different words wastes space and bores readers
Tangents: straying from your main argument (e.g., discussing unrelated tech examples)

example.label: Mistake Example
example.text: Weak: 'Technology is used by many people in the world. Many people use it every day. It's important.' No thesis, no examples, no argument. Grader scores 2–3

slides.warn: Each paragraph must advance your thesis; if a paragraph doesn't, delete it or integrate it.

slides.title: Time Management: 30 Minutes for an Essay
points: Minutes 1–2: read prompt, identify both viewpoints, brainstorm position
Minutes 3–5: outline (thesis + 2–3 body points + counter-arg). Write on test booklet
Minutes 6–27: draft 4–5 paragraphs. Don't aim for perfect; aim for complete
Minutes 28–30: proofread. Fix glaring errors; don't rewrite entire sentences

example.label: Time Allocation
example.text: Outline (5 min) → Draft intro + 2 body paragraphs (10 min) → Draft counter + conclusion (7 min) → Proofread (3 min). Total: 25 min, 5 min buffer

slides.tip: Writing a complete, imperfect essay is better than a polished 3-paragraph essay. Graders reward substance.

slides.title: Analyze an Issue: The Standard AWA Prompt
points: Prompt structure: 'Some argue X. Others argue Y. Discuss both sides and state your view.'
Your job: present both perspectives fairly, then argue your position with evidence
Avoid the 'Analyze an Argument' task (that's a different essay, not on modern GRE)
Modern GRE has ONLY 'Analyze an Issue'; the other task is no longer used

example.label: Issue Prompt Example
example.text: Prompt: 'Some believe that increasing automation will lead to widespread unemployment; others argue it will create new job categories. Discuss both views and present your own.' Essay: Intro (both views) → Body (evidence for job creation) → Counter (valid unemployment concern) → Conclusion

slides.tip: Understand prompt types; the modern GRE only tests 'Analyze an Issue.' (No argument essays.)

slides.title: Topic-Specific Examples: Tech, Education, Society
points: Technology: social media, automation, privacy, AI, digital divide
Education: standardized testing, online learning, traditional vs. progressive education
Society: immigration, economic inequality, free speech, globalization
Keep examples recent and relevant; timeless examples (Shakespeare, historical figures) also work

example.label: Example Arsenal
example.text: For tech prompt: ChatGPT/AI example. For education: remote learning post-pandemic. For society: social movements using digital platforms. Combine personal observation + current events

slides.tip: Build a list of 5–10 strong, versatile examples before test day; you'll reuse them.

slides.title: Advanced: Nuanced Positioning
points: Don't just pick a side; pick an angle: 'X is true in context A but false in context B'
Example: 'Technology isolates people in developed nations but connects isolated communities in developing regions'
This shows sophisticated thinking; graders reward context-awareness
Stronger than flat agree/disagree

example.label: Nuanced Thesis
example.text: Weak: 'Technology connects people.' Better: 'Technology's impact on human connection is context-dependent: it enhances collaboration among dispersed professionals but may diminish face-to-face depth in social relationships. On balance, the gains outweigh the losses in modern society.'

slides.tip: A 6-level essay often uses conditional framing (if, when, where) that acknowledges complexity.

slides.title: Avoiding Overconfidence: The Humility Factor
points: Absolute language ('always,' 'never,' 'all') is risky; use 'often,' 'generally,' 'typically'
Hedge your claims slightly: 'It is reasonable to argue...' or 'One could contend...'
This doesn't weaken your essay; it shows intellectual maturity
Graders respect writers who acknowledge complexity

example.label: Balanced Language
example.text: Weak: 'Technology always isolates people.' Better: 'Technology often creates isolation in social contexts, particularly when it replaces face-to-face interaction without intentional effort to maintain connection.'

slides.tip: Strong writers qualify claims; weak writers make sweeping statements they can't defend.

slides.title: Proofreading Under Time Pressure
points: Scan for the BIG issues first: misplaced modifiers, subject-verb disagreement, run-on sentences
Grammar: fix obvious errors (spelling, tense consistency, pronoun reference)
Don't obsess: minor errors (a/an, comma placement) don't tank your score
If you're unsure of a word's spelling, change it to a word you're confident about

example.label: Priority Fixes
example.text: High priority: 'The team were' → 'The team was' (subject-verb). Medium: comma splice. Low: 'utilize' vs. 'use' (either is fine). Skip low-priority items if time is tight

slides.tip: One final pass for clarity: does each sentence make sense? If not, simplify it.

slides.title: Sample High-Scoring Essay Structure
points: Intro (3–4 sentences): both views + clear thesis
Body 1 (5–7 sentences): claim + specific example + why it matters
Body 2 (5–7 sentences): second supporting claim + example + analysis
Counter-argument (3–4 sentences): concede opposing view, reframe your position
Conclusion (3–4 sentences): restate thesis, bigger implications, memorable closing

example.label: Full Essay Skeleton
example.text: Intro: ~50 words. Body 1: ~100 words. Body 2: ~100 words. Counter: ~60 words. Conclusion: ~50 words. Total: ~360 words (lean) to ~550 words (robust). Both are acceptable

slides.tip: Word count ranges: 350–600 words. More isn't better; substance is what counts.

slides.title: Grading Process: Human + AI Evaluation
points: Both human rater and AI score the essay. If scores differ by >1 point, a second human rates it
Final score is average of two human scores (or human + AI average)
Graders scan for: thesis clarity (immediately visible), evidence quality, reasoning coherence
Writing quality matters for score, but logic matters more

example.label: Scoring Scenario
example.text: Human scores 5.5. AI scores 5.0. Final = 5.25. If they scored 5.5 and 4.0 (>1 pt diff), second human rates; final = (5.5 + 5.0) / 2 or (5.5 + 4.0) / 2

slides.tip: Graders have read thousands of essays; they spot a strong thesis and solid evidence instantly.

slides.title: What Score Do You Need?
points: Top schools: 5.0–6.0 competitive (5.0 is solid; 5.5+ is strong)
Mid-tier schools: 4.5+ sufficient; AWA is often secondary
Many schools ignore AWA entirely; focus on Verbal + Quant for admissions
But a 5.5–6 essay can strengthen a borderline application

example.label: Score Interpretations
example.text: 6.0: Exceptionally articulate, insightful, well-developed. 5.0: Well-reasoned, clear, competent. 4.0: Adequate but weak. <4: Problematic logic or writing.

slides.tip: A 5.0+ is your target. Spend your prep time on Verbal + Quant first; they carry more weight.

slides.title: Practice Strategy for AWA
points: Week 1–2: read 3–5 sample essays (ETS official samples); identify strong vs. weak essays
Week 3–4: write 2–3 untimed essays; focus on structure and evidence
Week 5: write 2–3 timed essays (30 min); build pacing stamina
Week 6: review error patterns; refine your template (intro, 2 bodies, counter, conclusion)

example.label: AWA Practice Schedule
example.text: Monday: Read 1 sample essay + analyze. Wednesday: Untimed essay. Friday: Timed essay (30 min). Sunday: Review + refine outline template

slides.tip: AWA requires less prep than Verbal/Quant (since it's lower-stakes), but consistency matters.

slides.title: Free AWA Resources
points: ETS Official GRE Guide: includes sample prompts and scored essays with grader comments
ETS website: https://www.ets.org/gre/revised_general/prepare → writing topics + samples
Reddit r/GRE: community shares essays for feedback
Your grad school advisor or writing center: free feedback on practice essays

example.label: Free Resource Path
example.text: Read ETS samples (understand scoring). Write 1–2 practice essays. Share on r/GRE for peer feedback. Refine based on comments. Repeat 2–3 cycles

slides.tip: Don't overthink AWA; a competent 4.5–5.0 essay is sufficient for most programs.

slides.title: Top Mistakes in AWA Essays
points: Fence-sitting: 'Both sides are valid' without taking a stance → automatic 4.0 cap
No examples: abstract arguments without concrete evidence → graders downgrade
Unbalanced essay: spend 90% of space on one side, ignore the other
Unclear thesis: grader can't identify your position → confusion = low score

example.label: Mistake Impact
example.text: Mistake: Spend 3 paragraphs on side A, 1 sentence on side B, no clear position. Result: 3.5–4.0 (incomplete engagement). Fix: acknowledge both sides evenly, then argue your position = 4.5–5.5

slides.warn: Graders penalize incomplete engagement with the prompt. Address both viewpoints.

slides.title: GRE AWA: Final Tips
points: Confidence in your structure = faster writing. Memorize your 5-paragraph template
Examples are your essay's skeleton; without them, your argument collapses
It's okay if your writing isn't literary; clear and logical beats flowery and confusing
On test day: read prompt carefully, brainstorm for 2 min, outline for 3 min, write 20 min
slides.tip: Most students underestimate AWA then scramble at the end. Practice early; it pays off.
slides.warn: A sloppy essay (typos, unclear logic, weak examples) scores 3–4. Invest time in one good draft.

slides.title: Next: Integrated Prep Plan
points: Week 1–3: Verbal drills + 1 AWA practice essay
Week 4–5: Quant drills + 1 more AWA essay
Week 6–7: Full practice tests (Verbal + Quant + AWA together)
Week 8: Final mock + targeted review based on weakest section

example.label: 8-Week Plan
example.text: Weeks 1–3: Verbal 60%, Quant 30%, AWA 10%. Weeks 4–5: Quant catch-up. Weeks 6–7: Balanced practice tests. Week 8: Final mock + final review
